items.title: Nicole C. Mullen Gets Candid About Sin, Betrayal, and God
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Encouraging.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Singer Nicole C. Mullen is on a mission to inspire people to make “godly decisions.”

Mullen said her new book, “It’s Never Wrong to Do the Right Thing: Courageous Stories to Inspire Godly Decisions,” was written to inspire others to look to the Lord as they navigate their lives.

“I love it that it says over in Matthew 6:33, it gives us the formula,” she said. “It tells us to seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness — His right way of doing things, His right standing, and then He promises that everything else that we need, whether it’s relationships, finances, whether it’s health, whether it’s mental sanity … whatever it is that we need will be added.”

Mullen said her book intends to encourage people in this area, explaining how being candid and sharing her journey with sin and struggle is helpful to others. This meant opening up about domestic violence, betrayal, and other personal matters.

Listen to the latest episode of “Quick Start”

“I know that even in my weakness, Christ is strong,” she said. “I say all the time, ‘Lord, I bring my weakness to the table,’ and sometimes it comes with embarrassing moments. Sometimes it comes with me not looking as good as I would want to look. But at the end of the day, He’s always the hero; He’s always the champion.”

Mullen said she shared some personal anecdotes and stories in the book for that very reason. The singer pointed back to Scripture, too, where some raw and candid stories often show people’s flaws.

“Even in the Scriptures, I find that there are no perfect people except one … and that’s Christ Himself,” she said. “Everybody else was messed up. Everybody else … just made horrible decisions and all kinds of things, but I find that, when they sought God — when they did it His way, He gave them success through it, even if it didn’t turn out the way they thought.”

With that in mind, Mullen said she brought together numerous stories showing this very dynamic in her book, “It’s Never Wrong to Do the Right Thing.”

“I wanted to pull out everyday people to show us that we don’t have to be famous to make the right decision and have great impact,” Mullen said. “We just have to be found faithful to do what God has called us to do in the moment, and, when we do that, and oftentimes it’s in scary situations — it’s in difficult times.”

When we’re faced with right or wrong, Mullen said God will show up and give us what we need.

“Even if we don’t see it in the moment, we can trust God to know that He’s working together for our good and the benefit of other people as well,” she said.

Ultimately, Mullen said Christians must show up and “seek first the Kingdom of God” in any and all seasons.

“The Bible speaks to everything,” she said. “Even though the cultures may have been different, human nature … still the same. We still face the same fears, the same temptations, the same desires, the same insecurities.”

Find out more about Mullen’s book, “It’s Never Wrong to Do the Right Thing.”

items.title: God Sees All
items.author: Leslie Koh
items.summary: Michael couldn’t help laughing as Grace hid behind a menu. They were playing a game of hide-and-seek at the table in a café while waiting for the food. The five-year-old thought that if she couldn’t see her father, then he couldn’t see her. It seemed silly at the time, but a
items.content:
📖 Devotional | Our Daily Bread

Michael couldn’t help laughing as Grace hid behind a menu. They were playing a game of hide-and-seek at the table in a café while waiting for the food. The five-year-old thought that if she couldn’t see her father, then he couldn’t see her. It seemed silly at the time, but as Michael reflected on the incident later, he realized it contained an important lesson: Do we believe we can hide our sins from God? Do we think that if we can’t see Him, then He can’t see us?

In Amos 9, this same point is made when God, speaking through the prophet, warns Israel not to think they can escape judgment for their sins. “Though they hide themselves . . . I will hunt them down.” He said, “I will keep my eye on them” (vv. 3-4). Nothing escapes the eyes of the all-seeing, all-knowing God.

But the warning also came with a message of hope. In verses 11-15, God promises restoration: “I will restore David’s fallen shelter—I will repair its broken walls” (v. 11). After suffering the consequences of their sin, God’s people would be restored and given bountiful blessings (vv. 13-15).

Just as God sees our failings, He also sees our repentance, and He is ready to forgive and restore. As we draw comfort from this truth, let’s hold on tightly to the holy and righteous God who is full of mercy and grace.

items.title: Fighting for You
items.author: Karen Pimpo
items.summary: Professional boxer Jim Braddock was known as someone who fought not for riches and fame, but to put food on the table for his family. The movie Cinderella Man chronicles his fairytale-like comeback from a past-his-prime boxer to the world heavyweight champion. While facing extreme poverty during the
items.content:
📖 Devotional | Our Daily Bread

Professional boxer Jim Braddock was known as someone who fought not for riches and fame, but to put food on the table for his family. The movie Cinderella Man chronicles his fairytale-like comeback from a past-his-prime boxer to the world heavyweight champion. While facing extreme poverty during the Great Depression, Jim repeatedly sacrifices his own resources, health, and pride to provide for his children. He’s never intimidated by an opponent and courageously endures pummeling in the ring to keep his family safe.

Jim’s legacy is one of passionate defense of his family. We too, have a passionate defender who has promised to take our place in the ring. When the Israelites faced Pharaoh’s mighty army after their escape from slavery in Egypt, they were terrified and cried out to God. “It would have been better for us to serve the Egyptians than die in the desert!” they foolishly said (Exodus 14:12). But Moses replied in faith: “The Lord will fight for you; you need only to be still” (v. 14). And without any action from the Israelites, their enemies were literally swept away by the sea as God supernaturally ended the battle before it even began.

Sometimes it feels like we’re facing the trials of life or arrows from the enemy, Satan, on our own. But God has promised never to leave us or forsake us (Deuteronomy 31:6). He fights for us; we need only to be still.

items.title: ‘We’ve Done a Bad Job of Just Telling People to Pray About It’: Mike Todd on What the Church Gets Wrong About Trauma
items.author: Emily Brown
items.summary: Mike Todd’s biggest trauma had nothing to do with tragedy. The pastor of Transformation Church in Tulsa, Oklahoma, spent years unable to let anything just be good. Good had to become great, and the pressure to keep outperforming himself cost him his joy. “The Mike Todd definition of trau
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

Mike Todd’s biggest trauma had nothing to do with tragedy.

The pastor of Transformation Church in Tulsa, Oklahoma, spent years unable to let anything just be good. Good had to become great, and the pressure to keep outperforming himself cost him his joy.

“The Mike Todd definition of trauma is simply anything that impacts you greatly,” Todd said. “A lot of times, people think trauma is just bad things. But I talk about the trauma of success, because that impacted me greatly.”

By that definition, Todd said, almost nobody is walking around trauma-free — a coach who cut you in seventh grade, a sibling who never stopped saying “stop touching my stuff,” getting into the school you dreamed about and feeling nothing once you’re there.

“In this exact moment, so many different people are going through hard situations,” Todd said. “Especially since 2020, so many people have been discouraged in business, in parenting, in relationships, you name it.”

“In the church, we’ve done a bad job of just telling people to pray about it,” Todd said. “I do believe prayer is a catalyst and it is the ointment around all of the hard work that we have to do. But I don’t think it’s a cure-all fix-all one-time thing.”

He watched it play out in youth ministry, when teenagers would leave an altar call convinced they were changed for good.

“I can’t tell you how many people were like, ‘Oh, I feel different now,'” Todd said. “And I was like, ‘Yes, you feel different now, so do a different step now. Go to counseling, go to therapy.'”

What he’s asking for instead starts with acknowledgment.

“Most people are so aware of everybody else’s problems that they won’t admit their own,” Todd said. “If you don’t acknowledge something, you’ll never change it.”

He suggests starting small: the calls you avoid, the patterns you repeat, the reasons you keep certain people at a distance — and tracing them back to where they started.

On what the church owes people once they open up:

“We don’t have to solve it. We’re not the savior,” Todd said. “Most people feel intimidated by people’s problems because they think they have to fix it. You don’t have to fix anybody’s problem. You just have to point them to the One who can fix the problem.”

He credits four years of counseling with his wife for the rest of it.

“The more that I’m doing my own work, go to counseling, participate in small group, talking and processing things with my wife, it’s easier for me to be there for people who are going through the same thing,” Todd said.

Todd has talked publicly about a years-long addiction to pornography. What broke it, he said, was telling someone.

“I remember being so deep in that valley of perversion and thinking, will I ever be free from this?” Todd said. “Actually saying something about it, confessing to the community I was around, that was the hardest battle for years. But once that dam broke, help started coming. Now it’s been a decade and a half.”

That pattern, Todd said, holds for trauma of any size.

“What’s not transformed is transferred,” Todd said. “If you don’t deal with your trauma, it’s going to someone else.”

He points to the biblical language around generational sin.

“If you can’t figure out how to deal with your issues for yourself, consider the ones you love and actually deal with it for them,” Todd said. “There are people on the other side of your healing, as well as on the other side of your damage.”

Todd said the difference between white-knuckling through pain and facing it has changed how he experiences ordinary life.

“I feel like I’m really living now,” Todd said. “I’ve gotten to slow down and notice how full of favor my life is because I’m not trying to white-knuckle my way through everything anymore. If something hurts, I acknowledge that it hurt.”

“It’s almost like you’re watching something in black and white, and then the color comes in,” Todd said. “That’s what life is on the other side of healing.”

He won’t say healing arrives on a schedule.

“Every failure has the potential to turn into something in your favor,” Todd said. “On the other side of your greatest hurdle is a great victory.”

items.title: With Euthanasia Romanticized on TikTok, the Saxophones Are Getting Louder
items.author: Nora Kenney Mittiga
items.summary:
Nora Kenney Mittiga

Gen Z remains surprisingly attached to our culture’s almost obsessive commitment to individual autonomy, clinging to a worldview that treats suffering and dependence as problems to be eliminated.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Nora Kenney Mittiga

It’s chilling to recognize that Medical Aid in Dying (MAID) is enjoying a moment in the spotlight on TikTok—one that will likely continue to grow. The social media platform known for encouraging users to “romanticize” mundane daily life—from morning routines to Pilates workouts—is now casting the warm glow of its viral songs and amusing taglines on a procedure deliberately intended to end patients’ lives. 

Photogenic twenty-somethings with golden-blond hair, who look like they should be headed to “Bama Rush,” are instead documenting a “last day with grandpa,” to wistful “sadcore” music in the background. An account called “Anita’s Legacy,” with a Canadian flag in its name, originally focused on cooking and hospitality content, now claims to be dedicated to the memory of its original creator, dead through MAID. In an oddly chipper pinned video, Anita speaks directly into the camera: “I have passed away,” she says, explaining that the video was recorded before her death and given to her daughters to post posthumously. Another user, “wheredidbecsgo,” documented her journey toward MAID for an audience of over 100,000 followers. After being diagnosed with early-onset Alzheimer’s disease, she died through MAID in July, according to her page, posting a final goodbye video on the 22nd.

Comments responding to these types of videos are overwhelmingly supportive. “She’s taking control over how she wants to spend the last part of her life. That’s beautiful and incredibly brave,” one user commented on a video about a terminally ill grandmother. “May her passing be beautiful, celebrated, and on her own terms. Rest in power,” said another. 

But don’t be fooled by “vibes.” This trend is appalling. Not only is it jarring for an unassuming TikTok consumer—innocently scrolling through sun-drenched vacation vlogs and Herbie Hunkele’s spellbinding Lil Wayne cover—to encounter a morbid video from a perfectly conscious individual casually planning his or her own death. (What song will be playing? What scented candles will be lit? Who will be in the room?) But, more importantly, it’s disturbing that we’ve gotten to the point in which MAID itself is being optimized and packaged for content, with family and friends participating in—and even celebrating—the process. 

How did we get here? Assisted dying is hardly new, but in recent years, MAID has moved with remarkable speed from the margins of political debate toward the mainstream. Nowhere is the shift more apparent than among our neighbors to the north, as Canada has become the “euthanasia capital of the world.” But here in America, state by state, MAID is also gaining ground. Thirteen states now allow MAID, with New York becoming the latest to legalize it. After a decade-long legislative battle, the law, signed by Catholic governor Kathy Hochul, took effect in August.

Fortunately, many are pushing back. In New York, some of the most striking opposition to euthanasia has come from Catholic nuns who have devoted their lives to caring for the sick and dying. Four orders of religious sisters—the Dominican Sisters of Hawthorne, the Carmelite Sisters for the Aged and Infirm, the Missionary Sisters of St. Benedict, and the Little Sisters of the Poor—are now suing the state, arguing that its new MAID regime would force them to facilitate the very deaths their ministries exist to accompany gracefully. Bishop John Barres of the Diocese of Rockville Centre is a plaintiff alongside the sisters, and the broader New York Catholic hierarchy has rallied behind them. The New York State Catholic Conference was a prominent opponent to the law during the legislative fight, and Cardinal Timothy Dolan and Archbishop Ronald Hicks have publicly criticized it as well.

It’s understated, but there’s also pushback against the worldview of euthanasia on the silver screen. In Father Stu (2022), Hollywood all-star Mark Wahlberg portrays the true story of a boxer-turned-priest diagnosed with a devastating degenerative disease that gradually robs him of his physical capacities. While the film does not take an explicit stance on euthanasia (nor does it need to), it also refuses to treat suffering or dependence as evidence that life has lost value. Instead, Stu’s bodily decline becomes inseparable from his vocation and, in many ways, deepens it. The movie Wildcat (2023), about Flannery O’Connor, similarly testifies to the numinous power of suffering to bestow mysterious grace. The scene in which she discusses her lupus battle with her priest (played by Liam Neeson) is unforgettable. We need more stories like these.

And even on TikTok, pushback against MAID is slowly, timidly materializing. This matters, because TikTok is precisely where euthanasia can most perniciously and subtly be romanticized by unfamous, ordinary accounts. Big pro-life voices with millions of followers, like Matt Fradd and Lila Rose, are doing invaluable work warning audiences about the dangers of suicidal policies. But the normalization of MAID occurs at a different level: when average, non-celebrity influencers make ordinary-looking videos about a loved one’s goodbye, turning what should be an earth-shattering decision into something strangely unremarkable. Thus, we need resistance at that level too.  

Mario Zelaya, for example, is an entrepreneur and content creator in Canada. It’s unclear if he opposes MAID in all cases (he says, for example, in a July video, “I’m not here to pass judgment”), but in several videos, he decries observable signs that the practice does not always operate as carefully or equitably as defenders would suggest. A Salvadoran immigrant to Canada, Zelaya points out, for example, that white Canadians appear to use MAID at disproportionately higher rates than other racial groups—and that oftentimes, veterans and the mentally ill seem unfairly targeted. He makes the broader point that such stark demographic disparities should themselves raise questions about the entire practice.
Word on Fire’s Liturgy of the Hours is Here!
Order Your Set Today

Joseph Elfar, MD, is another everyday TikTok creator who has questioned the knee-jerk approval of MAID as a blanket solution in cases of physical or emotional discomfort. “Offering compassion for somebody does not include validating self-destructive or life-ending ideas,” he explained in a May video, describing the use of permanent solutions for what may be temporary conditions as “unethical.” (Requests for comment sent to Zelaya and Elfar were unanswered.)

Physician-assisted suicide is not romantic. It should not be flippantly promoted through trending audios or medical-tourism framing. The creators on TikTok who most vocally defend it—and states that offer it—often invoke the language of “death with dignity,” as does popular pro-euthanasia creator (and New York Times best-selling author) “Hospice Nurse Julie” (Julie McFadden, RN). But that description could not be further from the truth. Real dignity doesn’t have to mean foregoing pain medication or using every available means to prolong life when death is inevitable, but it does mean honoring the full range of the human condition—including suffering and dependence—that God allows us to experience. 

The support for MAID among young people, as demonstrated on TikTok, is particularly jarring. In other areas of cultural life, younger generations have shown at least some signs of becoming “post-woke”—exhibiting fatigue with certain excesses of “peak woke,” which seems to have apexed around 2020. Think of corporate rainbow-logo campaigns every June, indigenous land acknowledgments, Christopher Columbus statue protests, tedious pronoun rituals, cancel campaigns over minor comments, and the once-reflexive defense of transgender participation in women’s sports. These types of efforts are now regularly mocked by Gen Z, and in some cases dismissed as “boomerisms.” But unfortunately, if TikTok is any indication, this post-woke skepticism has not extended to their feelings on the progressive sacred cow of euthanasia. 

Why is that? Is it possible that they have thoroughly internalized the logic of efficiency culture, even as they so famously denounce workism? Paradoxically, Gen Z may bristle at the idea that a worker’s value lies in his productivity—penning essays against “hustle culture,” championing “quiet quitting,” and transforming “girlboss” from an aspiration into an insult—but they remain surprisingly attached to our culture’s almost obsessive commitment to individual autonomy, clinging to a worldview that treats suffering, dependence, and diminished efficiency as problems to be eliminated. 

And this is not going away. A 2025 Siena College poll of New York voters showed that 54 percent of respondents ages 18 to 34 supported legislation allowing doctors to prescribe lethal drugs to terminally ill patients for the purpose of assisted suicide. This matched the support of older generations (54 percent among those aged 35 to 54, and 55 percent among those 55 and older). But opposition was also weakest among the youngest respondents: just 23 percent of 18-to-34-year-olds opposed the idea, compared with 30 percent and 29 percent, respectively, among those ages 35 to 54 and 55 and older.

These findings should set off alarm bells—or as the kids say on TikTok, “the saxophones are getting louder.” 

In his final column for the New York Times, Ross Douthat acknowledged his sustained criticism of the “elite consensus” of technocratic and social liberalism and its tendency toward “overreach.” “Even when it started out in a reasonable place it didn’t know when to stop, and there was too much about human nature that it didn’t seem to know,” he wrote. MAID is one of the darkest expressions yet of this tragic—shall we say, decadent—ignorance. Americans possess extraordinary medical technology and unprecedented material comfort; yet increasingly, when confronted with suffering and dependence, our answer is not to deploy these resources to accompany the sufferer but to hasten death. Or in TikTok’s case, to romanticize it. 

Like Douthat, G. K. Chesterton understood keenly that material sophistication was no guarantee against moral barbarism. “Some of the most civilized and highly organized cultures, like Carthage at its wealthiest, had human sacrifice at its worst,” he wrote. TikTok creators, of course, would be playing wistful music while decadent Carthage inevitably fell. 

When it comes to physician-assisted suicide—to the normalized, unremarkable deaths of ordinary grandparents—medicine can make the process painless. Social media can present it as aesthetic and empowering. The state, obliviously, can call it dignified. But none of these veneers can ever fully absolve euthanasia of its fundamental violation of God’s plan for his children.

Dr. Tod Worner

How did a poor immigrant boy from Brooklyn rise to become Yale’s Sterling Professor of Classics and History, achieve fame as the world’s greatest scholar on Thucydides, and find himself compared to none other than Herodotus? Even more, how did he cultivate the wisdom of a mentor, the devotion of a father, and the kindness of a friend? Join Hillsdale Professor Paul Rahe and me as we explore the incredible journey and unlikely genius of Donald Kagan on The Evangelization & Culture Podcast.
